topic: Why Compression Is Prediction: The Information-Theoretic View of LLMs

key_points: Compressors and LLMs solve the same core problem: building a probabilistic model of data to minimize the bits needed to represent it.
Explains the three 'organs' of a compressor: transforms, models (symbol probabilities), and entropy coders (arithmetic/Huffman coding).
Shannon entropy is the floor for lossless compression; avg bits/symbol = entropy, computed via -log2(probability).
Context matters: an order-1 model (previous symbol as context) cuts compressed output by more than half vs. no context.
LLMs are next-token predictors: given context they output a probability distribution over tokens, then a token is chosen and appended (fancy autocomplete).
Using an LLM for compression: feed context, look at the probability the model assigns to the ACTUAL next token; cost in bits = -log2(that probability).
A well-trained model assigns high probability to the real next symbol => few bits; a bad model assigns low probability => many bits.
Concrete comparison: order-1 model compresses a Dickens quote to 434 bits (24% of original); GPT-2 with arithmetic coding to 176 bits (10%).
Why LLMs aren't used everywhere: resource constraints — both server and client would need the multi-GB model; gzip/Brotli overhead is tiny by comparison.
2023 DeepMind paper argues language modeling and compression are two views of the same thing.
DeepMind 'Language Modeling Is Compression' (Delétang et al., 2023): predictive models can be transformed into lossless compressors and vice versa.
Chinchilla 70B, trained primarily on text, compresses ImageNet patches to 43.4% and LibriSpeech samples to 16.4% of raw size.
Beats domain-specific compressors: PNG (58.5%) and FLAC (30.3%) respectively.
Compression viewpoint gives novel insights into scaling laws, tokenization, and in-context learning.
Prediction-compression equivalence lets any compressor (e.g., gzip) be used to build a conditional generative model.
Advocates viewing the prediction problem through the lens of compression.
Hutter Prize rewards data-compression improvements on enwik9 (1 GB of English text) to encourage AI research.
Launched 2006 by Marcus Hutter; awards 5,000 euros per 1% improvement (500,000 euros total funding).
Organizers believe text compression and AI are equivalent problems.

Hutter proved optimal behavior of a goal-seeking agent in an unknown computable environment is to guess the environment is controlled by one of the shortest programs consistent with all interaction so far.
Kolmogorov complexity is not computable, so there is no general solution.
Compression is a concrete, measurable proxy for intelligence/prediction quality.
Gwern's directory on compressed transformers and context compression: DeepSeek-OCR optical compression, Cached Transformers, In-Context Autoencoder, Gist Tokens for prompt compression.
Connects LLM compression with information theory and practical prompt/context compression techniques.
Covers how context/attention can be compressed to cut inference cost while preserving performance.
Carlini's well-known essay 'GPT is a data compressor' demonstrates using GPT-2 to losslessly compress text via arithmetic coding on its token probabilities.
Shows prediction quality maps directly to compression ratio — a practical, measurable proof of the prediction-compression link.
Popularized the idea in the ML community that LLMs are essentially very good compressors of natural language.

stats.fact: The Hutter Prize (launched 2006) offers 5,000 euros per 1% compression improvement on enwik9, with 500,000 euros total funding, explicitly treating text compression as equivalent to AI.
Chinchilla 70B, trained primarily on text, compresses ImageNet patches to 43.4% of raw size, beating PNG (58.5%).
Chinchilla 70B compresses LibriSpeech audio samples to 16.4% of raw size, beating FLAC (30.3%).
GPT-2 with arithmetic coding compresses a classic Dickens passage ('It was the best of times...') to 176 bits, about 10% of the original; an order-1 statistical model needs 434 bits (24%).
In English, the letter 'U' has probability ~0.028 overall, but ~0.999 when preceded by 'Q' — context raises probability from ~5.158 bits to ~0.001 bits per symbol.
Bits required to encode a symbol = -log2(probability). Shannon entropy is the theoretical floor for lossless compression.

angles: The 'aha' reframe: training an LLM and writing a compressor are the same task — both build a probability distribution over data to minimize bits.
From entropy coding to next-token prediction: arithmetic/Huffman coding uses symbol probabilities exactly like an LLM uses token probabilities.
Compression as a measurable proxy for intelligence (Hutter Prize) and for model quality — better predictor = better compressor.
Practical implication: the same loss function (cross-entropy ≈ compressed bits) drives both model training and compression, linking LLM scaling to information theory.
Why we don't compress the web with LLMs today: resource constraints (multi-GB models on both ends) vs. tiny gzip/Brotli overhead.
Emerging frontier: using LLM probability estimates to compress prompts/context (gist tokens, in-context autoencoders) and the compression-view insights into scaling laws and tokenization.
